subject: physics
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} question that tests this idea: "{lo}". Then score my answer the way an AP reader would.
promptWeak: Explain this {board} idea simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake students make: "{lo}".

questions.q: An astronaut drifts 3 m from a space station, far from Earth and all other bodies. Which statement about the gravitational interaction between the astronaut and the station is correct?
options: Neither pulls the other, since gravity is zero in empty space.
They attract each other with forces of equal magnitude.
The station pulls her, but she exerts no pull on the station.
Each pulls the other, but the station’s pull on her is the larger.
optionWhy: A student who thinks there is no gravity in space picks this. Any two masses attract, wherever they are; empty space between them does not stop the interaction.

The gravitational force is attractive and mutual: the station pulls the astronaut toward it and she pulls the station toward her. The magnitudes are both Gm_am_s/r², although the force is far too small to notice.

A student who thinks only the larger body attracts picks this. Gravity is an interaction between two masses, so if the station pulls the astronaut, she pulls the station with a force of equal magnitude.

A student who thinks the more massive object exerts the larger force picks this. The two forces have the same magnitude, Gm_am_s/r²; the station’s much larger mass gives it a much smaller acceleration, not a smaller force.
questions.explain: The gravitational force is attractive and mutual: the station pulls the astronaut toward it and she pulls the station toward her. The magnitudes are both Gm_am_s/r², although the force is far too small to notice.

questions.q: A spacecraft coasts with its engines off past an asteroid, far from all other bodies. In which direction is the gravitational force exerted on the spacecraft by the asteroid?
options: Toward the asteroid’s center, along the line joining them
Straight down, in the one fixed direction of “down” everywhere
Along the spacecraft’s velocity, in its direction of motion
There is none, since the asteroid has no atmosphere at all
optionWhy: The gravitational force is attractive and is exerted along the line connecting the centers of mass of the two objects, so it points from the spacecraft toward the asteroid’s center.
A student who thinks gravity always points “down” picks this. Far from Earth there is no fixed down; the force points toward the center of the object exerting it, here the asteroid.

A student who thinks a moving object has a force along its motion picks this. With the engines off, the only object interacting with the spacecraft is the asteroid, which pulls it toward the asteroid’s center.
A student who thinks gravity needs air picks this. Every object with mass exerts a gravitational force; an airless asteroid attracts the spacecraft just as a planet would, only more weakly.
questions.explain: The gravitational force is attractive and is exerted along the line connecting the centers of mass of the two objects, so it points from the spacecraft toward the asteroid’s center.

questions.q: Point P is in the air 2 m above the ground near Earth’s surface, and no object is at P. Which statement about the gravitational field at P is correct?
options: There is no field at P until an object is placed there to feel it.
It is 10 N/kg for a 1 kg object at P and stronger for a heavier one.
It is about 10 N/kg toward Earth’s center, object or no object.
It exists at P only because the air surrounding P transmits Earth’s pull.
optionWhy: A student who thinks a field needs an object to exist picks this. The field is created by Earth at every point around it; a test object only reveals it.
A student who thinks the field depends on the test mass picks this. A heavier object has a proportionally larger force, so the force per unit mass, the field, is the same, about 10 N/kg.

A field models the noncontact force at every point in space. Earth sets up its gravitational field at P whatever is there; an object placed at P would simply experience a force of about 10 N per kilogram of its mass.
A student who thinks gravity needs air picks this. Gravity is a noncontact force that acts through empty space; the field at P would be the same with no air.
questions.explain: A field models the noncontact force at every point in space. Earth sets up its gravitational field at P whatever is there; an object placed at P would simply experience a force of about 10 N per kilogram of its mass.
questions.working: The field at P is set up by Earth whether or not anything is there: |g⃗| = GM/r² ≈ 10 N/kg near the surface, directed toward Earth’s center. An object of mass m placed at P would have a force of about (10 N/kg)m exerted on it; the ratio F/m does not depend on m, and no medium is needed.

questions.q: Near the surface of Earth, the gravitational field strength is g ≈ 10 N/kg. Which statement correctly interprets this value?
options: The field there is about 10 N/kg for a 1 kg object, and is larger for heavier objects.
Every object near Earth’s surface has a gravitational force of about 10 N on it.
The field has this value of about 10 N/kg at any distance from Earth’s center, near or far.
Earth exerts about 10 N of gravitational force on each kilogram of an object there.
optionWhy: A student who thinks the field depends on the object placed in it picks this. A heavier object has more force on it, but the force per kilogram, the field, is the same.
A student who confuses the field with the force picks this. 10 N/kg is a force per kilogram; a 5 kg object has about 50 N on it, a 0.1 kg object about 1 N.
A student who thinks g is a universal constant picks this. The value applies near the surface; farther from Earth’s center the field is GM/r², which is smaller.

A field strength in N/kg is a force per unit mass: near the surface, an object of mass m has about (10 N/kg)m of gravitational force exerted on it, and if gravity is the only force it accelerates at about 10 m/s².
questions.explain: A field strength in N/kg is a force per unit mass: near the surface, an object of mass m has about (10 N/kg)m of gravitational force exerted on it, and if gravity is the only force it accelerates at about 10 m/s².
questions.working: g = F_g/m, so 10 N/kg means 10 N of gravitational force per kilogram: a 5 kg object has about 50 N exerted on it. The ratio does not depend on the object’s mass, and the value holds only near the surface, since the field is GM/r².

questions.q: The figure shows a cross section of a thin, uniform spherical shell with center O, far from all other objects, and a small object at point P inside the shell. What is the net gravitational force exerted on the object by the shell?
options: Toward the right side of the shell, since that part is nearest to P
Toward the left side of the shell, since more of its mass is on that side
Zero, because the pulls of all the parts of the shell cancel out
Toward O, as if all of the shell’s mass were concentrated at point O
optionWhy: A student who thinks the nearest part of the shell pulls hardest picks this. More of the shell’s mass is on the far side, and its larger mass exactly offsets its larger distance, so the net force is zero.
A student who counts only how much mass is on each side picks this. That larger mass is also farther away; at every point inside a uniform shell the opposite pulls cancel exactly.

Newton’s shell theorem: the net gravitational force exerted by a thin uniform shell on an object anywhere inside it is zero. The nearer part of the shell is closer but has less mass in each direction, and the pulls cancel exactly.
A student who treats the shell as a point mass at its center everywhere picks this. That model holds only outside the shell; inside, the net force from the shell is zero.
questions.explain: Newton’s shell theorem: the net gravitational force exerted by a thin uniform shell on an object anywhere inside it is zero. The nearer part of the shell is closer but has less mass in each direction, and the pulls cancel exactly.

questions.q: A brick slides across a level concrete floor on its largest face, which has three times the area of its smallest face. The brick is then turned onto its smallest face and slides across the same floor at twice the speed. What is the ratio of the kinetic friction force on the brick in the second case to that in the first case?
optionWhy: A student who takes the friction force to be proportional to the contact area picks this: one third of the area gives one third of the force. The friction force depends on the normal force, which is unchanged.

On a level floor the normal force equals the brick's weight on either face, and the coefficient depends only on brick and concrete. In this model |F⃗_f,k| = μ_k F_N depends neither on the contact area nor on the speed, so the ratio is 1.00.

A student who reasons that a smaller face presses harder and so has more friction picks this. The force per unit area is three times larger, but the total normal force, which sets the friction, is the same.
A student who thinks kinetic friction grows with sliding speed picks this. μ_k F_N contains no speed, so doubling the speed leaves the kinetic friction force unchanged.
questions.explain: On a level floor the normal force equals the brick's weight on either face, and the coefficient depends only on brick and concrete. In this model |F⃗_f,k| = μ_k F_N depends neither on the contact area nor on the speed, so the ratio is 1.00.
questions.working: F_f,k = μ_k F_N with F_N = mg in both cases (level floor, no other vertical forces). Neither area nor speed enters, so F₂/F₁ = (μ_k mg)/(μ_k mg) = 1.00.

questions.q: A crate sits on the flat bed of a truck. The truck speeds up from rest along a straight, level road, and the crate does not slip on the bed. Which statement correctly describes the horizontal force on the crate?
options: Kinetic friction from the bed acts backward, since the crate is moving.
Static friction from the bed acts forward, the way the crate accelerates.
No horizontal force acts; the crate is carried along by the truck.
Static friction from the bed acts backward, opposite to the crate's motion.
optionWhy: A student who calls friction kinetic whenever the object moves relative to the ground picks this. The crate does not slide on the bed, so the friction is static, and it must point forward to speed the crate up.

The crate and the bed do not move relative to each other, so any friction between them is static. The crate speeds up forward, so the net horizontal force on it points forward, and the only horizontal force is static friction from the bed.
A student who thinks an object can be carried along without a force picks this. The crate's velocity changes, so a net force acts on it; the bed exerts it through static friction.

A student who thinks friction always opposes an object's velocity picks this. A backward force would slow the crate down; static friction points forward here, in the direction of the crate's velocity.
questions.explain: The crate and the bed do not move relative to each other, so any friction between them is static. The crate speeds up forward, so the net horizontal force on it points forward, and the only horizontal force is static friction from the bed.

questions.q: For a given pair of dry surfaces, such as a wooden crate on a concrete floor, how does the coefficient of static friction μ_s typically compare with the coefficient of kinetic friction μ_k?
options: μ_s < μ_k, so a crate is harder to keep sliding than to start it
μ_s > μ_k, so a crate is easier to keep sliding than to start
μ_s = μ_k, since both describe the same two surfaces in contact
It depends on the crate's mass, as a heavier crate presses harder
optionWhy: A student who thinks sliding surfaces grip harder picks this. The everyday observation is the opposite: the push needed drops once a heavy box starts to move.

For a given pair of surfaces μ_s is typically greater than μ_k. The push needed to start a crate sliding, μ_s F_N, is therefore larger than the push needed to keep it sliding at constant speed, μ_k F_N.

A student who thinks one pair of surfaces has one coefficient picks this. The two coefficients describe different situations, surfaces not slipping and surfaces sliding, and typically μ_s is the larger.
A student who thinks a coefficient changes with the load picks this. A heavier crate has a larger normal force, which changes both friction forces, but neither coefficient.
questions.explain: For a given pair of surfaces μ_s is typically greater than μ_k. The push needed to start a crate sliding, μ_s F_N, is therefore larger than the push needed to keep it sliding at constant speed, μ_k F_N.

questions.q: The diagram shows a block held at rest by a horizontal string tied to a wall while a conveyor belt slides beneath it in the direction shown. Which statement describes the friction force exerted on the block by the belt?
options: Kinetic friction, directed to the left
Static friction, directed rightward
Kinetic friction, acting to the right
No friction, since the block is at rest
optionWhy: A student who thinks friction opposes whatever motion is happening, here the belt's motion to the right, picks this. Friction on the block opposes the block's motion relative to the belt, which is to the left, so it points right.

A student who calls friction static whenever the object is at rest relative to the ground picks this. The block's surface slides over the belt's surface, so the friction is kinetic, even though the block is at rest.

The block's surface and the belt's surface move relative to each other, so the friction is kinetic. Relative to the belt, the block moves to the left, so kinetic friction on the block points to the right, opposite to that relative motion; the string's pull to the left balances it.

A student who thinks friction acts only on moving objects picks this. The belt slides under the block, and if there were no friction, nothing would balance the string's pull and the block would not stay at rest.
questions.explain: The block's surface and the belt's surface move relative to each other, so the friction is kinetic. Relative to the belt, the block moves to the left, so kinetic friction on the block points to the right, opposite to that relative motion; the string's pull to the left balances it.

questions.q: A 20 kg box is pulled across a level floor by a rope that exerts a 100 N force directed 37° above the horizontal. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the box and the floor is 0.30. Use g = 10 m/s². What is the magnitude of the kinetic friction force on the box?
optionWhy: Vertically, F_N + (100 N) sin 37° = mg, so F_N = 200 N − 60 N = 140 N. Then |F⃗_f,k| = μ_k F_N = 0.30 × 140 N = 42 N. (The horizontal pull, 80 N, exceeds this, so the box speeds up.)

A student who takes the normal force to equal the weight, 200 N, picks this: 0.30 × 200 N = 60 N. The rope's upward component, 60 N, supports part of the weight, so the floor pushes up with only 140 N.
A student who thinks kinetic friction balances the horizontal pull picks this: (100 N) cos 37° = 80 N. Kinetic friction is μ_k F_N = 42 N whatever the pull; the difference accelerates the box.

A student who uses the cosine component as the rope's vertical component picks this: F_N = 200 N − 80 N = 120 N and 0.30 × 120 N = 36 N. With the angle measured from the horizontal, the vertical component is (100 N) sin 37° = 60 N.
questions.explain: Vertically, F_N + (100 N) sin 37° = mg, so F_N = 200 N − 60 N = 140 N. Then |F⃗_f,k| = μ_k F_N = 0.30 × 140 N = 42 N. (The horizontal pull, 80 N, exceeds this, so the box speeds up.)

questions.q: The diagram, not drawn to scale, shows three arrangements, X, Y and Z, of identical ideal springs supporting identical blocks at rest. Δx_X, Δx_Y and Δx_Z are the distances each block is below the position it would have if its springs were relaxed. Which ranking is correct?
options: Δx_Z > Δx_X > Δx_Y
Δx_X = Δx_Y = Δx_Z
Δx_X = Δx_Y > Δx_Z
Δx_Y > Δx_X > Δx_Z
optionWhy: A student who swaps the rules, adding constants in series and reciprocals in parallel, picks this: Y would be 2k and Z would be k/2. Springs side by side share the load, so Z is the stiffest arrangement.
A student who gives any combination of identical springs the average constant, k, picks this. Two springs in series make a softer combination (k/2) and two side by side a stiffer one (2k).

A student who thinks the load is shared between the springs in Y, as it is in Z, picks this: each spring of Y would stretch mg/(2k), a total of mg/k. Each spring in series carries all of mg, so Y stretches 2mg/k.
With spring constant k for each spring, X has k, Y (series) has k/2 and Z (parallel) has 2k. For the same weight, Δx = mg/k_eq, so Y stretches 2mg/k, X mg/k and Z mg/(2k).
questions.explain: With spring constant k for each spring, X has k, Y (series) has k/2 and Z (parallel) has 2k. For the same weight, Δx = mg/k_eq, so Y stretches 2mg/k, X mg/k and Z mg/(2k).
questions.working: X: k_eq = k → mg/k. Y (series): 1/k_eq = 2/k → k_eq = k/2 → 2mg/k. Z (parallel): k_eq = 2k → mg/(2k). Δx_Y > Δx_X > Δx_Z.

figure.alt: Three arrangements hanging from a horizontal ceiling, not drawn to scale, each holding an identical block. X: one spring from the ceiling to the block. Y: two springs joined end to end, one below the other, between the ceiling and the block. Z: two springs side by side, each running from the ceiling to the same block. All the springs are identical.

questions.q: A spring of mass m_s hangs from a ceiling, and a block of mass M hangs at rest from its lower end. The spring is not ideal, because its mass is not negligible. If g is the acceleration due to gravity, what is the magnitude of the force exerted by the ceiling on the spring?
options: Mg
(M + m_s/2)g
m_s g
(M + m_s)g
optionWhy: A student who treats the spring as transmitting only the load, as an ideal spring would, picks this. The spring's own weight also hangs from the ceiling, so the force at the top exceeds the force at the bottom by m_s g.

A student who thinks the spring's weight is shared between its two ends picks this. The lower end is attached to the block, which pulls down; only the ceiling holds the spring up, so it supports the whole of m_s g.
A student who thinks the ceiling holds up only the spring it touches picks this. The block hangs from the spring, which hangs from the ceiling, so the ceiling supports both weights.

Take the spring and block together as the system. It is at rest, and the only forces on it are its total weight, (M + m_s)g, and the ceiling's upward force, so the ceiling exerts (M + m_s)g. The spring pulls on the block with only Mg, so the force differs from one end of the spring to the other.
questions.explain: Take the spring and block together as the system. It is at rest, and the only forces on it are its total weight, (M + m_s)g, and the ceiling's upward force, so the ceiling exerts (M + m_s)g. The spring pulls on the block with only Mg, so the force differs from one end of the spring to the other.
questions.working: System = spring + block, at rest: F_ceiling − Mg − m_s g = 0 → F_ceiling = (M + m_s)g. (Block alone: the spring's lower end pulls up with Mg; spring alone: F_ceiling = Mg + m_s g.)

questions.q: An ideal spring has a relaxed length of 0.10 m. A force of 1.2 N holds it stretched to a length of 0.12 m. What force must be exerted on the spring to hold it stretched to a length of 0.16 m?
optionWhy: Hooke's law uses the change in length from the relaxed length. k = 1.2 N/(0.12 m − 0.10 m) = 60 N/m. At 0.16 m the change in length is 0.06 m, so the force is (60 N/m)(0.06 m) = 3.6 N.

A student who takes the force to be proportional to the spring's total length picks this: (1.2 N)(0.16 m/0.12 m) = 1.6 N. The force is proportional to the change from the relaxed length, which triples from 0.02 m to 0.06 m.
A student who measures the further stretch from the 0.12 m length picks this: (60 N/m)(0.04 m) = 2.4 N. Δx is always measured from the relaxed length, 0.10 m, so it is 0.06 m.
A student who thinks a spring exerts a fixed force picks this. The spring's force grows in proportion to its change in length, so a larger stretch needs a larger force.
questions.explain: Hooke's law uses the change in length from the relaxed length. k = 1.2 N/(0.12 m − 0.10 m) = 60 N/m. At 0.16 m the change in length is 0.06 m, so the force is (60 N/m)(0.06 m) = 3.6 N.

questions.q: A block on a frictionless, horizontal surface is attached to an ideal spring whose other end is fixed to a wall. The diagram shows the block at x = 0, where the spring is relaxed, and three other positions of the block, P, Q and R; +x is to the right. F_P, F_Q and F_R are the x-components of the spring force on the block at P, Q and R. Which ranking is correct?
options: F_R > F_Q > F_P
F_P > F_Q > F_R
F_R > F_P > F_Q
F_P = F_Q = F_R
optionWhy: A student who takes the spring force to point the same way as the displacement, F = +kx, picks this. The spring force points back toward x = 0, opposite to the displacement.

F_x = −kx. At P (x = −0.10 m) the compressed spring pushes right: F_P = +0.10k. At Q (+0.05 m) and R (+0.20 m) the stretched spring pulls left: F_Q = −0.05k and F_R = −0.20k. In signed values, F_P > F_Q > F_R.
A student who ranks the sizes of the forces (0.20k, 0.10k, 0.05k) instead of their x-components picks this. At R the force points left, so its x-component, −0.20k, is the smallest of the three.

A student who thinks a spring exerts the same force wherever the block is picks this. The force is proportional to the change in the spring's length and points toward x = 0, so it differs at the three positions.
questions.explain: F_x = −kx. At P (x = −0.10 m) the compressed spring pushes right: F_P = +0.10k. At Q (+0.05 m) and R (+0.20 m) the stretched spring pulls left: F_Q = −0.05k and F_R = −0.20k. In signed values, F_P > F_Q > F_R.

questions.q: A 4.0 kg block hangs from an ideal spring of spring constant 100 N/m attached to the ceiling of an elevator. The block is at rest relative to the elevator, which has an upward acceleration of 3.0 m/s². Use g = 10 m/s². By how much is the spring stretched from its relaxed length?
optionWhy: A student who takes the spring force to equal the weight picks this: (40 N)/(100 N/m). That holds only when the block does not accelerate; here the spring must also supply the net upward force ma.

A student who thinks an upward acceleration lightens the block picks this: (4.0 kg)(10 − 3.0) m/s²/(100 N/m). An upward acceleration needs a net upward force, so the spring pulls harder than the weight.
The block accelerates upward with the elevator, so the net force on it is up: kΔx − mg = ma. Δx = m(g + a)/k = (4.0 kg)(13 m/s²)/(100 N/m) = 0.52 m.
A student who sets the spring force equal to ma picks this: (4.0 kg)(3.0 m/s²)/(100 N/m). ma is the net force; the spring must also balance the weight, mg.
questions.explain: The block accelerates upward with the elevator, so the net force on it is up: kΔx − mg = ma. Δx = m(g + a)/k = (4.0 kg)(13 m/s²)/(100 N/m) = 0.52 m.
questions.working: Up positive: kΔx − mg = ma → Δx = m(g + a)/k = (4.0 kg)(10 m/s² + 3.0 m/s²)/(100 N/m) = 0.52 m.

questions.q: A ball is thrown straight up, and air resistance on it is not negligible. The diagram shows the ball's velocity at two instants, P and Q. Which describes the direction of the resistive force exerted on the ball by the air at P and at Q?
options: Upward at P and upward at Q
Downward at P and upward at Q
Zero at P and upward at Q
Downward at P and downward at Q
optionWhy: A student who thinks air resistance always opposes gravity picks this. It opposes the velocity: while the ball rises, the air pushes it down, adding to gravity's effect.
A resistive force points opposite to the object's velocity. At P the ball moves up, so the force points down; at Q the ball moves down, so the force points up.
A student who thinks air resistance acts only on falling objects picks this. The ball moves through the air at P too, so a resistive force acts, opposite to its upward velocity.

A student who gives the resistive force the direction of the net force picks this. The net force is downward at both instants, but at Q the resistive force alone points up, against the downward velocity.
questions.explain: A resistive force points opposite to the object's velocity. At P the ball moves up, so the force points down; at Q the ball moves down, so the force points up.

questions.q: A skydiver falls at her terminal velocity. Which statement about the skydiver is correct?
options: Gravity is slightly larger than the resistive force, keeping her moving.
Air resistance balances her weight, so the net force on her is zero.
No forces act on her now, because her velocity is no longer changing.
Her acceleration is at its maximum, since her speed is at its maximum.
optionWhy: A student who thinks motion needs a net force in its direction picks this. Any unbalanced downward force would make her speed up; at constant velocity the forces balance.
Terminal velocity is reached when the net force is zero: the upward resistive force equals her weight in magnitude, so her velocity stays constant.
A student who reads 'zero net force' as 'no forces' picks this. Earth still pulls her down and the air still pushes her up; the two forces add to zero.
A student who links large acceleration with large speed picks this. Her speed is constant, so her acceleration is zero; it was largest, g, at the start of the fall.
questions.explain: Terminal velocity is reached when the net force is zero: the upward resistive force equals her weight in magnitude, so her velocity stays constant.

questions.q: A ball of mass m is thrown straight up and experiences a resistive force F⃗_r = −kv⃗. Upward is taken as positive, and g is the magnitude of the acceleration due to gravity. Which differential equation describes the ball's velocity v while it is rising?
options: dv/dt = −g + (k/m)v
dv/dt = +g − (k/m)v
dv/dt = +g + (k/m)v
dv/dt = −g − (k/m)v
optionWhy: A student who takes air resistance to point up, opposing gravity, picks this. While the ball rises its velocity is upward, so the resistive force, −kv, points down.
A student who reuses the falling-object equation, written with downward positive, picks this. With upward positive, gravity's term is −g.
A student who adds the sizes of the two forces, mg + kv, without signs for their directions picks this. With upward positive, both forces point down while the ball rises, so both terms are negative.
Newton's second law with upward positive: gravity contributes −mg, and the resistive force −kv points down while v is positive. So m dv/dt = −mg − kv, and dividing by m gives dv/dt = −g − (k/m)v.
questions.explain: Newton's second law with upward positive: gravity contributes −mg, and the resistive force −kv points down while v is positive. So m dv/dt = −mg − kv, and dividing by m gives dv/dt = −g − (k/m)v.
questions.working: Up positive: ΣF = −mg + (−kv) = m dv/dt → dv/dt = −g − (k/m)v. Units: k/m in 1/s, so (k/m)v in m/s².

questions.q: A 0.40 kg toy boat glides across still water in a straight line with its motor off. The water exerts a resistive force F⃗_r = −kv⃗ with k = 0.50 kg/s, and no other horizontal force acts. How long does it take the boat's speed to fall to half its initial value?
optionWhy: Separating variables in m dv/dt = −kv gives ∫dv/v = −(k/m)∫dt, so v = v₀e^(−kt/m). The speed halves when kt/m = ln 2: t = (m/k) ln 2 = (0.80 s)(0.693) = 0.55 s.
A student who keeps the deceleration at its initial value, kv₀/m, picks this: the speed would halve at m/(2k) = 0.40 s. The force shrinks as the boat slows, so halving takes longer.

A student who takes the time constant m/k = 0.80 s to be the time for the speed to halve picks this. At t = m/k the speed is e⁻¹ ≈ 0.37 of its initial value; it fell to one half earlier, at (m/k) ln 2.
A student who uses k/m as the time constant picks this: (1.25)(0.693) = 0.87. k/m has units of 1/s, not s; the exponent in the solution is −kt/m.
questions.explain: Separating variables in m dv/dt = −kv gives ∫dv/v = −(k/m)∫dt, so v = v₀e^(−kt/m). The speed halves when kt/m = ln 2: t = (m/k) ln 2 = (0.80 s)(0.693) = 0.55 s.

questions.q: Two balls of the same size and shape, so with the same resistive constant k, have masses m and 4m. Each falls with a resistive force F⃗_r = −kv⃗. What is the ratio of the terminal speed of the 4m ball to that of the m ball?
optionWhy: A student who extends 'all objects fall alike' to falls with air resistance picks this. That holds only when the resistive force is negligible; here the heavier ball needs a larger resistive force, and so a larger speed, to balance its weight.
A student who uses the quadratic-drag result, v_T ∝ √(mg), picks this: √4 = 2. For the linear model F⃗_r = −kv⃗, v_T = mg/k is proportional to the mass.
At terminal velocity the net force is zero: kv_T = mg, so v_T = mg/k. With the same k, v_T is proportional to the mass, and the ratio is 4m/m = 4.00.

A student who thinks the heavier ball has more air resistance and so falls more slowly picks this. The resistive force depends on speed, not mass; the heavier ball must reach a higher speed before kv equals its weight.
questions.explain: At terminal velocity the net force is zero: kv_T = mg, so v_T = mg/k. With the same k, v_T is proportional to the mass, and the ratio is 4m/m = 4.00.
questions.working: Terminal condition: kv_T − mg = 0 → v_T = mg/k. Ratio (4m)g/k ÷ mg/k = 4.00.
